lessons.title: Addresses
intro: Three registers aren't much. That's why the 6502 has memory: up to 65,536 boxes of one byte each. Every box has an address from $0000 to $FFFF.
Our board has 1 KB of RAM, $0000 to $03FF. Your program is loaded at $0200, so we keep our data at $0300 and up, where it can't overwrite the code.
Here's the most important rule: with # you mean a number, without # you mean an address. LDA #$30 loads the number $30. LDA $30 loads whatever is stored at address $30.

exercises.prompt: How many bytes fit into one memory address?
exercises.explanation: Each address holds exactly one byte, a number from $00 to $FF.

exercises.prompt: What is the highest address the 6502 can use?
exercises.explanation: Addresses have 16 bits, so they go from $0000 to $FFFF (65,535).

options: Loads A with the byte stored at address $0300
exercises.explanation: Without #, the value is an address. LDA $0300 looks into box $0300 and copies its contents into A.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between LDA #$30 and LDA $30?
options: #$30 is the number, $30 is the byte at address $30
exercises.explanation: # means "this number". Without #, the 6502 goes to that address and reads what's there.

exercises.prompt: Load A with the byte stored at address $0300.
exercises.explanation: No # here: we want the contents of address $0300, not a number.

exercises.prompt: Where does your program start on our board?
exercises.explanation: Programs are loaded at $0200. That's why we use $0300 and up for data.

lessons.title: STA: Store
intro: STA $0300 stores A into memory: address $0300 gets a copy of A. A keeps its value. STX and STY store X and Y.
You can't put a number straight into memory. You load it into a register first, then store the register: LDA #7, then STA $0300.
STA never uses #. A number isn't a place to store something, so STA #$0300 makes no sense to the 6502.

exercises.prompt: After this program, what's in $0300 and in A?
exercises.explanation: STA copies A into memory. The value stays in A as well.
STX stores the X register. STA would store A, which is still 0 here.

exercises.prompt: This program stops with an error. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: STA needs an address, not a number. Remove the #: STA $0300.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that stores 9 at $0300 and 4 at $0301.
exercises.explanation: Every value goes through A: load it, then store it. Each LDA has to come right before its own STA.
Both STA lines write to $0300. The second one overwrites the first, so $05 is left.

exercises.prompt: Which program puts 1 into $0300 without changing A?
exercises.explanation: Using X leaves A alone. LDA #1 would change A.

lessons.title: Loading from Memory and Zero Page
intro: LDA $0300 reads a byte from memory into A. Load and store together let you copy memory: LDA $0300, then STA $0301.

Addresses $0000 to $00FF are special: the zero page. You can write them with two digits, like $30. Those instructions are shorter (2 bytes instead of 3) and faster, so programmers keep their most used values there.
LDA $30 and LDA $0030 read the same box. The short version simply saves a byte.

exercises.explanation: The first two lines store $0C at $0300. LDA $0300 reads it back, STA $0301 copies it on.

options: The first line of a program
exercises.explanation: The zero page is the first 256 bytes. Its addresses fit in one byte, which makes instructions shorter.

exercises.prompt: Why do programmers like the zero page?
options: Instructions there are shorter and faster
It's the only memory you can store to
exercises.explanation: LDA $30 needs 2 bytes, LDA $0300 needs 3. On a 1 MHz chip with 1 KB of RAM, that matters.
LDA $30 reads it into A, STA $31 writes A to the new address.

exercises.prompt: This program should copy the byte at $0300 to $0301, but it stops with an error. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: LDA #… loads a number. To read memory, leave out the #: LDA $0300. (A number this big doesn't even fit into A.)

exercises.prompt: Build a program that copies the byte at $10 to $20.
exercises.explanation: First read into A, then write A to the new address.
